v.rationale: impl-2 ranks first. Its core path (ledger and status) never depends on Acme's API, the card fetch is a separately retried job, and both exactly-once and out-of-order protection are done with atomic SQL that holds up on several MySQL servers. It is the only implementation that is right on both sub-second ordering and UTC offsets, its error responses are always JSON, and its tests are the most thorough. Its gaps are about recovery: a card fetch whose dispatch is lost is never retried, and there is no sweeper. impl-1 is close behind, with the most idiomatic L13 code (queue and model attributes, FormRequest, signature middleware) and a solid atomic-claim sweeper. It loses ground on real but smaller bugs: offsets aren't normalised and a test asserts the wrong ordering, validation failures get 302 redirects when there is no Accept header, and the ledger waits on the Acme lookup. impl-3 is last. It has a fat controller with hand-written validation, no FormRequest or middleware, `$guarded = []` on every model and string literals instead of enums. It also has confirmed bugs: microseconds are truncated so sub-second ordering is wrong, a null card_last4 keeps an event out of the ledger permanently, firstOrCreate races under concurrent deliveries, and the sweeper piles up duplicate jobs. All three suites pass (25, 23 and 13 tests), and all three overwrite the payment amount with a partial refund's amount.

The webhook route is in the web group, so a failed FormRequest validation gives Acme a 302 redirect to the previous page instead of a 4xx. Probes saw this when Content-Type was missing, when an unknown event type had no `occurred_at`, and when an unknown type had non-array `data`. Acme gets a 302 and retries for 24 hours. The ledger write and status update sit in the same job as the card_last4 fetch. While Acme's API is down, the ledger and status are not updated for hours. That meets 'work happens once it is back', but money bookkeeping ends up depending on an enrichment call.

I ran each suite (all pass: impl-2 23, impl-3 13, impl-1 25) and probed each implementation with throwaway tests, which I deleted afterwards.

**impl-2 (rank 1)** has the soundest webhook design. The signature middleware checks the raw bytes and fails closed. It acknowledges straight away and stores the raw payload. One atomic transaction claims the event, writes the ledger and runs a conditional UPDATE keyed on `last_event_at`, with microseconds and UTC handled correctly. The card fetch is a separate job retried for 24 hours, so an Acme outage never holds up the ledger. Its weaknesses are small: the fetch job is dispatched after commit with no recovery path, and ProcessAcmeEvent has a 5-try limit and no sweeper.

**impl-1 (rank 2)** is the most idiomatic Laravel 13 code: a FormRequest with `requiredIf`, enums, attributes everywhere, createOrFirst, and a sweeper with a `dispatched_at` claim. But a probe showed timezone offsets stored as wall-clock time, so an older event with a +02:00 offset overwrote a newer UTC event. Its own offset test passes only by coincidence. Because the route is in the web group, failed validation sends Acme a 302 redirect. Probes saw this for a missing Content-Type and for unknown event types without `occurred_at`. It also writes the ledger only after the Acme API fetch succeeds.

**impl-3 (rank 3)** has the heaviest controller: signature checking, decoding, hand-written validation and persistence all in one place, with no middleware, no FormRequest, `$guarded = []` and string constants instead of enums. It also has two confirmed correctness bugs. Microseconds are dropped by the datetime cast, so a newer event in the same second is ignored. A `null` card_last4 from Acme makes the job throw, so the ledger entry is never written.

Both suites pass (46 and 43 tests). impl-1 has the more idiomatic Blade and model layer: form components (input/select/textarea/checkbox) built on @props, $attributes->class and @error; price formatting on the model; exact string-to-cents conversion; LIKE wildcards escaped; broader tests. But it fails a stated requirement. The checkbox component has no hidden 0 field, so when an admin unticks 'Active' on the create form and the submit fails, old('is_active') is null and the box re-renders ticked. A probe confirmed this. impl-2 handles that case with a hidden input and has no requirement failures. It adds a slug field with Rule::unique()->ignore(), an enum for sort with Rule::enum, @session, whereLike, whereBelongsTo and Model::shouldBeStrict. Its weaknesses: Number::currency with a fully qualified class name repeated in three views, filter selects and the textarea written inline instead of as components, LIKE wildcards not escaped, and float-based cents conversion. Both send invalid filter query strings back to '/' with no error shown. Because real bugs are weighted heavily, impl-2 ranks first despite impl-1's somewhat better idioms.

v.rationale:
All three have the same core design. The command catches Throwable for each id, calls report(), adds the product id through Context and returns FAILURE when any id fails. The HTTP client maps ConnectionException and 5xx to PartnerDown and calls throw() for 4xx. Errors are throttled with `$exceptions->throttle(Limit::perMinute(3)->by(class))`. The probes found one real difference: maintenance mode. impl-1 and impl-3 register /live without exempting it from PreventRequestsDuringMaintenance, so it returns 503 during `artisan down`. Between impl-1 and impl-3, impl-1 is better built: /live sits outside the web group in `then:`, the DB check is a discovered listener class, it sets connectTimeout, and it has the most thorough tests. impl-3 puts /live in web.php and strips the group with withoutMiddleware('web'), which is more hacky, though its PartnerDown messages are the most detailed. - a 422 invalid-address response
- a partner that keeps answering 503 until retries run out

- the global limit of 5 requests per second

- payment done as a conditional update inside a transaction, with the job dispatched only after commit
- a queue rate limit of 5 per second for the whole account
- no overlapping runs for the same order
- retries bounded by time rather than attempt count
- queue attributes for backoff, maximum exceptions and timeout
- an idempotency key sent to the partner
- failure handling that never overwrites a shipment that already exists

- A unique index on the shipment reference.
- It records a 422 as a failed shipment without putting an entry in failed_jobs.
- Its failure reasons are readable and truncated, where impl-2 stores the raw exception message.
- markAsPaid returns a bool.
- Its tests are more rigorous: transaction rollback, the serialize round-trip used to check cancelled orders, datasets, and rendering the email.

- Its email claim is rolled back if sending fails, which is closer to exactly-once than impl-1's claim-then-queue (impl-1's small real bug).
- Its rate-limit test checks behaviour rather than structure.
- It is a little simpler, with no separate service class.

**Against impl-2:**
- No unique index on the shipment reference.
- It uses fail() for an expected business outcome, which adds noise to failed_jobs.
- Two tests are misleading: one named for exactly-once email never runs the retry, and one named for retry exhaustion relies on the sync driver calling failed() straight away.

v.rationale: The two implementations share nearly the same core code: the same named rate limiter keyed by lowercased email and IP, the same FormRequest, controllers and routes. Both test suites pass (impl-1: 20 tests, impl-2: 17). The difference that decides the ranking came from probing. In impl-1, a client that sends no `Accept: application/json` header gets a 500 'Route [login] not defined' on GET /api/me and DELETE /api/auth/token instead of a 401. The focus area asks for correct status codes for every client, and a mobile client could easily leave that header out. impl-2 found this, fixed it in bootstrap/app.php with redirectGuestsTo, and tested both request styles. Both still return 500 when `email` is an array, because the throttle key reads raw input before validation. impl-2 has small weaknesses: a no-op `RateLimiter::clear` and no email format rule. These count for much less than impl-1's real 500 on a common client path. Throttling works the same way in both: 6th attempt blocked, separate counts per email and per IP, case-insensitive, reset after a minute. Neither leaks secrets.
